_meta.description: Academic-domain personas curated following the PersonaHub methodology (Ge et al., 2024). Each persona is a short natural-language description of a person's role, expertise, and perspective, used as a prompt prefix to diversify synthetic query generation.
_meta.reference: Ge, T., Hu, X., Wang, L., Chen, S., & Yu, D. (2024). Scaling Synthetic Data Creation with 1,000,000,000 Personas. arXiv:2406.20094
_meta.curation_note: These personas are domain-adapted for academic document understanding (ML/AI/fairness). When HuggingFace access is available, replace or augment with personas sampled directly from PersonaHub persona.jsonl.

personas.persona: A third-year PhD student researching algorithmic fairness who is preparing for their qualifying exam and needs to deeply understand how different fairness metrics interact with model performance across demographic groups.

A senior research scientist at a major AI lab who specializes in natural language processing and is reviewing papers for a top-tier conference, looking for methodological gaps and overclaimed contributions.

A machine learning engineer at a mid-size tech company evaluating whether to adopt a new method in production, primarily concerned with compute cost, data requirements, latency constraints, and whether reported gains hold on real-world benchmarks.
An undergraduate computer science student reading their first machine learning research paper, struggling with mathematical notation and needing concrete examples to understand abstract concepts.
A government policy analyst specializing in AI ethics and regulation who reads technical papers to extract policy-relevant implications, particularly around bias, transparency, and accountability.
A statistician with expertise in experimental design who is skeptical of machine learning papers that lack proper statistical testing, confidence intervals, or ablation studies.
A computer science professor preparing lecture materials for a graduate seminar on trustworthy AI, looking for clear examples and illustrative figures to explain complex concepts to students.

A data scientist at a healthcare startup who needs to understand fairness-aware methods to comply with regulatory requirements, prioritizing practical implementation details over theoretical contributions.
A technology journalist writing an article about AI bias for a general audience, looking for key findings and real-world implications that can be explained without heavy jargon.

A postdoctoral researcher in computer vision exploring how fairness constraints affect visual recognition systems, interested in cross-modal evidence linking model architectures to performance disparities.
A PhD student in theoretical computer science who focuses on the mathematical foundations of machine learning and wants to verify whether the proofs and formal claims in a paper are rigorous.
An experienced conference reviewer known for thorough and critical reviews, who systematically checks whether baselines are fair, experiments are reproducible, and limitations are honestly disclosed.

The CTO of an AI startup who skims papers quickly to assess whether a technique could give their product a competitive edge, caring mainly about the bottom-line performance numbers and implementation complexity.
A research librarian helping graduate students find relevant papers, who needs to understand a paper's core contribution and relationships to other works to provide accurate recommendations.
A philosophy professor specializing in ethics of technology who reads ML papers to assess whether the operationalization of fairness aligns with philosophical definitions of justice and equity.
A PhD student working on reinforcement learning who reads fairness papers to understand whether similar bias mitigation techniques could apply to sequential decision-making settings.
A quantitative analyst at a financial firm exploring whether fairness-aware machine learning methods could be adapted for regulatory compliance in credit scoring and lending decisions.
A researcher attempting to reproduce the results of a paper, meticulously checking every hyperparameter, dataset split, and evaluation protocol to identify potential sources of discrepancy.
A tenured professor with heavy administrative duties who only has 15 minutes to skim a paper before a committee meeting and needs to quickly grasp the main contribution and its significance.

A medical informatics researcher evaluating whether a fairness-aware ML method could be applied to clinical prediction models, concerned about patient safety and healthcare-specific regulatory constraints.
A second-year PhD student writing their first literature review on algorithmic fairness, trying to categorize papers by methodology and understand how different approaches compare.

An applied ML researcher at a national laboratory who cares about scaling methods to large datasets and distributed computing environments, often questioning whether elegant small-scale results survive at scale.
A legal consultant advising tech companies on AI compliance who reads technical papers to translate algorithmic fairness concepts into language suitable for legal frameworks and corporate policies.
A researcher organizing a workshop on responsible AI who is surveying the field to identify emerging trends, open problems, and potential invited speakers.

A computational social scientist studying how algorithmic systems affect marginalized communities, who reads ML papers with a critical eye toward whether the studied populations and metrics reflect real-world harms.
A first-year master's student in data science who has taken introductory ML courses but finds research papers intimidating, especially the mathematical formulations and dense related work sections.

A researcher who maintains a popular fairness benchmark suite and reads new papers to determine whether proposed methods should be added as baselines, focusing on reproducibility and standardized evaluation.
A product manager at a tech company who needs to understand AI fairness research to make informed decisions about which methods to prioritize in their product roadmap.

A visiting scholar from a developing country who is adapting fairness-aware methods to local contexts where data distributions, demographic categories, and regulatory environments differ significantly from Western settings.
An independent ML researcher without institutional affiliation who relies on clearly written papers and open-source code to stay current, and is frustrated by papers that omit implementation details.
A patent examiner reviewing AI-related patent applications who needs to determine whether a method described in a paper constitutes prior art for a pending patent claim.
A robotics engineer exploring how fairness constraints in perception models affect safety-critical autonomous systems, particularly interested in worst-case performance across different environments.
A researcher working at the intersection of NLP and fairness who is looking for transferable techniques from computer vision fairness papers that could apply to language model debiasing.
A research lab manager who assigns reading groups and needs to quickly assess whether a paper is suitable for junior students or requires senior-level background knowledge.
A principal investigator writing a grant proposal on trustworthy AI who reads recent papers to cite as motivation and position their proposed work within the current research landscape.
A PhD student preparing a 20-minute presentation of a paper for their research group's weekly reading seminar, needing to extract the key ideas, strengths, and weaknesses.
A corporate AI auditor tasked with evaluating whether deployed ML models meet fairness standards, who reads academic papers to understand the theoretical basis of the metrics they must verify.
An online course instructor creating educational content about AI fairness for a non-technical audience, looking for intuitive explanations and compelling visualizations from papers.
A researcher who deliberately tries to find flaws in papers — checking for cherry-picked results, misleading visualizations, unfair baseline comparisons, and unstated assumptions.
A systems researcher who focuses on efficient ML infrastructure and reads fairness papers to understand the computational overhead of bias mitigation techniques at deployment scale.
A researcher specializing in dataset curation and documentation who evaluates papers for how well they describe their data sources, preprocessing steps, and potential biases in the training data.
A machine learning competition participant looking for novel techniques that could improve their submission's performance on fairness-constrained benchmarks.
A philosophy PhD student writing a dissertation on algorithmic justice who reads technical ML papers to ground their philosophical arguments in concrete algorithmic practices.
A busy senior researcher who only reads abstracts, figures, and tables — never the full text — and expects to grasp the main contribution from visual elements alone.
A computational biologist exploring whether fairness-aware methods from ML could address bias in genomic prediction models across different population groups.

An open-source developer who implements paper methods as reusable libraries, focused on API design clarity, edge case handling, and whether the paper provides enough detail for faithful reimplementation.
An HR technology analyst evaluating AI hiring tools for bias, who reads fairness research to understand what guarantees different debiasing methods can and cannot provide.
A researcher attending a poster session at a major AI conference who has exactly 5 minutes to understand each paper's contribution and decide whether to follow up.
A researcher conducting a meta-analysis of fairness methods across multiple papers, systematically extracting and comparing experimental setups, metrics, datasets, and reported results.
A software engineer with a growing interest in ML fairness who reads papers on weekends to self-educate, often confused by assumed background knowledge and field-specific terminology.
